desc:
Each meeting is a half-open time range [start, end), so a meeting ending at time 10 does not clash with one starting at time 10. Two meetings clash when they share at least one moment.

A meeting is in conflict if it clashes with at least one other meeting in the list (two identical meetings clash with each other). Return how many meetings are in conflict.

meetings = [[1, 5], [2, 3], [6, 8], [8, 9], [10, 12]]  ->  2

Only [1, 5] and [2, 3] clash with anything.
constraints: The meetings are in no particular order
hints: Checking every pair of meetings is a valid start, but there is a faster way after sorting.
Sort by start time. A meeting can clash with an earlier one, with a later one, or with both. How could you detect each of the two cases cheaply?

Keep the largest end time seen so far: if the current start is smaller than it, the meeting clashes with an earlier one. If the next meeting starts before the current one ends, it clashes with a later one.
editorial: After sorting by start time, meeting i clashes with some earlier meeting exactly when its start is smaller than the maximum end time among the earlier meetings. It clashes with some later meeting exactly when the very next meeting in sorted order starts before end[i], because that next meeting has the smallest start among all later ones.

So one pass with a running maximum end, plus a look at the neighbour, decides each meeting. Counting a meeting once even when it clashes in both directions is natural because you test the two conditions with or. Sorting makes it O(n log n) time with O(n) space.
solution:
def countConflicting(meetings):
    ordered = sorted(meetings)
    n = len(ordered)
    count = 0
    max_end = -1
    for i in range(n):
        s, e = ordered[i]
        if s < max_end or (i + 1 < n and ordered[i + 1][0] < e):
            count += 1
        max_end = max(max_end, e)
    return count
